subsubtopic: TARIFF ON RAW WOOL FOR THE PROTECTION OF HOME GROWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the object in view, namely the encouragement of sheep raising for the purpose of supplying wool to our factories, I fully sympathize. I quite agree with the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) who has just
taken his seat, that we have not done enough in that regard. In that part of the province of Quebec in which is situated the constituency I represent there is not the slightest doubt that very large tracts of land not fit for other purposes would be excellent sheep-raising grounds, and the same is true of very large portions of territory in other parts of Quebec and in Ontario and the maritime provinces. But as to the means propounded in the resolution for encouraging this industry I must say that I have some hesitation. I remember that in the past I advocated the same thing- putting up the duty on raw wool so as to encourage the raising of sheep; but after I had given more time and study to the question I came to the conclusion that that was perhaps not the best remedy for the situation.
First of all, speaking at least for eastern Canada, I think there has been too much neglect in the matter of the breeds of sheep which have been introduced into this country. Of late years something has been done by the government of the province of Quebec to encourage the breeding of good wool-growing sheep, but that is still a very feeble effort. As to the federal government, I remember last year receiving a letter from an agricultural organization in my county asking under what conditions they could secure from the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa the services of blood sires to improve their stock. I made inquiry and I found out that it would have been possible for them to get a stallion; but it seems to me that in the present state of things it is not the breeding of horses that should be encouraged but rather the breeding of sheep.
Much has been done by provincial organizations and by private organizations more or less connected with governments to improve the dairy herds by breeding good stock. Much progress has been made in that direction, but not enough has been done I think with regard to improving our breeds of sheep.
As to the qualities of wool, I have tried to inform myself as well as I could through Canadians or foreigners who are engaged in the industry, and I have been told-I do not give it as a fact myself because I am not an expert-that in order to produce certain qualities of woollen goods we still have to import foreign goods and that in exchange we export raw wool of a coarser quality. Whether in those parts of British Columbia, to which the hon. member for Yale has alluded, it is possible to raise the finest grades of sheep that give alpaca wool, for instance, I do not know, but of course my hon. friends from that part of the country know. As far as eastern Canada is concerned I do not think that either our climate or our soil is favourable to the raising
Canadian Wool Industry

of these finer breeds of sheep. Therefore we must consider the problem from the viewpoint of the whole of Canada, and for that reason I do not think that Canada can become a wool producing country to the same degree as Australia or New Zealand or India. Nevertheless something should be done.
There are various means at the disposal of both the federal and the provincial authorities which would meet the object of hon. gentlemen who are supporting this resolution, without resorting to that old and somewhat worn-out remedy of raising the tariff. I do not think it is necessary to raise the tariff; to do that would have a greater effect than the hon. member for Yale believes. We have already experienced the effects of the tariff. It is all very well to make calculations of the amount of duty actually levied on the quantity of wool that enters into the making of a suit of clothes, but as my hon. friend knows, by the time the raw article has been imported, manipulated and turned into manufactured goods, the amount of duty is trebled and quintupled and very often multiplied ten times for the benefit of the manufacturer or the tradesman, so that the consumer really pays more than the actual amount of the duty levied upon a certain portion of material entering into a manufactured article.
But I do not want to bring up again the whole question of protection. As I have stated frequently in the house, I have no bias on that question; I may say-cynically perhaps -that I have no principles on the question. I do not believe in the creed of protection or in the creed of free trade, but I do believe that in these days, considering the interests of Canada as a whole, more or less interwoven as they are with the interests of other countries, and considering the necessities of trade, the government should hesitate before applying the crude remedy of raising the tariff every time there is same complaint by the producer of an agricultural or manufactured product. This question should be studied more thoroughly. I understand that the National Research Council has made a study with regard to the quality of wools, to which the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser) made reference. I suppose their conclusions will bring some light on that one aspect of the question, as to the varieties of wool and the possibility of producing in Canada the finest quality of wool which is required for the finest articles. In that connection, however, hon. gentlemen must bear in mind the great change which has taken place in-shall I say?-the fancies of the people. In the old days, for example, the general demand was for wool, pure woollen goods both for undergarments

and for outside clothing, even for dresses. Well, I suppose the ladies are largely responsible for the change in our habits, because from day to day and from year to year they have been looking constantly for lighter and lighter articles, until they dress up, or rather dress down, even in winter to such an extent that the woollen industry has suffered largely through these changes in fashion. Even some men believe it is more healthy to wear a much lesser proportion of woollen undergarments than they did in the old days. I am one of the oldtimers; I still stick to wool, but it has become very difficult to get the real woollen articles .manufactured in Canada. I may tell the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryck-man) that every time I go to the other side I buy a shirt or two in England or France in order to be sure that I get a woollen shirt, because you cannot get them in Canada. The 'article which is sold in Canada as woollen is loot woollen, although there is some portion bf wool in it. So that is another aspect of the question.
Encouragement should be given to the breeder to raise better stock, by way of premiums or some other means which could be discussed between the federal and the provincial authorities, and the manufacturers also should be induced to make greater use of wool. My good friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) could make use of his fine spirit of .propaganda, and issue, not in any luxurious way, but in a practical way, not a creed, but some sound advice to the public of Canada to make use of an article which is suited to our climate. We are not living in Africa or in the tropics. We live in a cold climate, where woollen goods are a necessity, I consider. A good many of the illnesses that are going around among both sexes are due largely, although there are other causes, .to the fact that we have discarded the good woollen shirt and the good woollen under and upper garments.
I wish to direct my next few remarks to the discouragement of the small industries by large manufacturers. Without applying my remarks to any particular constituency or geographical circle, may I say that in the old days in the province of Ontario, the maritime provinces and most certainly in the province of Quebec, there were small woollen industries producing articles for local consumption. In my own constituency, for example, most of the goods used in the shanties by lumberjacks were made in the surrounding country. The manufacture of those woollens gave work to the people in the villages; many women were enabled to stay at home and work on these products, in that way fulfilling at once their

Canadian Wool Industry
social duties as mothers of families or daughters assisting their mothers, and helping a local trade.
What has been the course pursued by the large manufacturers? They have discouraged and hewn down the small factories. In my constituency the father of a family, an industrious man, thought he would be helping himself, his family and his community by establishing a small woollen industry. He purchased nothing but wool grown in the community, the work was performed by his sons and daughters and the cost of production was reduced to a minimum; but what happened? The minute he began to expand his trade and sell some of his articles in Montreal and Toronto he was immediately boycotted by the representatives of all the large factories. As a result his trade was ruined.
The successful endeavours of large monopolized industries to kill small local industries apply not only to wool but to many other commodities. If there is a desire to encourage the farmer to raise the proper kind of sheep to produce the best grade of wool there must be an endeavour to place at his disposal at the nearest possible point a small factory which will purchase his wool at a fair price and will not cut down the rate under the pretence that a large industry, bejng capable of purchasing in bulk quantities and importing from foreign countries, cannot afford to pay large prices to small farmers. They may urge the excuse that the small producer does not clean his wool properly. In my view it would be a very simple matter for manufacturers with good will in their hearts to teach the farmers the best manner in which to prepare their wool, so that uniformity, quality and cleanliness of product might be the result.
I have no intention of dealing at length with this subject, but wish simply to associate myself with the desire of the hon. member who sponsors this resolution. I suggest, however, in the most friendly spirit that I do not think the remedy proposed is quite sufficient, and in my view it would not have the result he anticipates.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate myself with this resolution, for three principal reasons. First, I am in favour of the protection of every sound industry in Canada, basic and manufacturing; second, because I represent a district very largely concerned with the raising of sheep and the production of wool; and, third, because of the loss to Canada of the woollen industry in general.
It is difficult for me to conceive of any industry which should be more typically Canadian, from the point of the original product to that of the very highest manufacturing, than the woollen industry. All across Canada there are areas ideally suited to the raising of sheep. Regardless of what may have been said I contend we live in a country where woollen goods are required, and everything that can be done should be done to foster our woollen industry. The question at once arises: Why has the industry, surrounded as it has been by every natural condition which should tend towards its development, languished? The answer is simply this: In the woollen industry, as in almost every other industry, no one in Canada has been able to [DOT]tell from year to year what was going to happen to the particular line of manufacturing in which he was engaged. For a short time there would be a protective tariff and at another period it would be taken away. The vacillating policy which was pursued has made it impossible for the man raising sheep to know what was going to happen in one, two, three or four years.
One or two questions have been raised with regard to the industry in general. An hon. member has asked why we export wool, and another has asked why we are importing it. We ask ourselves why we should export any portion of our wool and at the same time be importing the same product. The answer has been that our exports are of qualities not suitable for manufacture in Canada. Less than a year ago it was my privilege to attend a conference of wool growers and sheep raisers from different parts of Canada, and at that meeting I heard the reasons why we are exporting wool and, at the same time, importing. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Stewart) mentioned this afternoon the name of Mr. Rosamond of Almonte, a manufacturer of woollens who uses, very largely, Canadian wool. He said to that conference, "We manufacturers are anxious to use one hundred per cent Canadian wool, but we cannot get it. First, there is not sufficient wool produced for the present general requirements, and second, the industiy has been in such an unstable condition that it has not been possible to develop the type of industrial organization to take Canadian wool, and bring it to a point where it would be suitable for the manufacture of all classes of goods produced in Canadian woollen plants." It was pointed out at that conference that there was no combing or carding industry in Canada; consequently Canadian wool had to be sent out of the country for processing. So far as I know the same wool may come back in manufactured form. The statement was made that if there
Canadian Wool Industry

was an assurance of continuous and reasonable protection for the woollen industry, both producer and manufacturer, it would be possible to build in Canada that high type Of manufacturing plant capable of receiving the fleeces from Canadian producers and converting them into high grade woollens required by the most exacting manufacturers.
The statement has been made that Canadian manufacturers have dictated the extent of protection that the wool producer should receive. I know nothing about that, but I was told at the conference, composed partly of wool growers and sheep raisers, that a tariff doubling or trebling the price of Canadian wool to the manufacturer would be satisfactory. The manufacturers said they would continue to purchase Canadian wool in large quantities. In passing may I add that the grading of wool has added largely to the security of the manufacturer buying the raw product. Under present conditions he is in a position to secure any grade for which he may ask. Those manufacturers pointed out that even if the price of wool were doubled or trebled the cost of the raw product would be but a small item as compared with the cost of the finished article. To illustrate, one of the delegates said that the actual cost of the raw wool in the suit of any delegate present would represent only about twenty-five cents of the whole cost of the suit.
It may be said that although the woollen industry is languishing every other industry is in a similar plight. That may be true, but it is no reason why some attempt should not be made to stabilize this industry, indigenous as it is to almost every province of Canada, particularly the west and some areas in Ontario and Quebec. I may say that in the district I represent the area devoted to sheep raising could take care of all the sheep in Canada, if they were raised in the intensive way in which they raise sheep not only in England and Scotland, but also in Australia and New Zealand. That is an illustration of what may be possible.
This afternoon my hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Stanley) raised the point of developing industry to its highest point in Alberta. Nothing that the hon. gentleman said or could say was more pertinent than that statement. Anyone who has had the privilege of going through the province and seeing its possibilities-power, fuel, oil, with the tremendous areas available for sheep raising-must reach the conclusion that under any plan of reasonable encouragement Alberta should be the home not only for the raising of sheep, but also for the manufacture of

woollen goods for at least all the western part of the dominion.
I wish to associate myself with this resolution, Mr. Speaker, and to urge on the government, as strongly as I possibly can, favourable consideration of its subject matter, which has been supported so adequately by members on this side of the house.

You may
laugh, but I tell you they are doing it yet. Now the Saskatchewan Sheep Breeders' Association have passed a resolution, and this is the concluding paragraph:
Therefore be it resolved that we respectfully urge upon the government of Canada that the sheep breeding industry be encouraged and the wool growing business be protected by the enactment of a protective tariff on wool equal to the tariff on woollen yarns and semi-manufactured cloth.
My hon. friend is a farmer. Well, here is a whole bunch of six or seven hundred farmers. They have laid down a sort of feather tick so they can fall on it and not get hurt. We ask that this resolution be enacted so that the raw wool industry of Canada may be fully protected.
You say that the Conservative party has really gobbled up the province of Saskatchewan, and that this is probably a sort of political dodge. I have heard that suggestion before. To safeguard myself against anything 41761-27
of that kind, I wrote the secretary of the Sheep Breeders' Association and asked him to send me a copy of the resolution. I know the secretary very well; he and I are good personal friends. I refer ito Mr. J. G. Robertson. You ask: Who is Mr. J. G. Robertson? I tell you he is live stock commissioner for Saskatchewan under the provincial government. That sounds political, you say. It does. But he was appointed live stock commissioner by the late Liberal government and has been continued in office by the present government, although he is the rankest Grit in the province. He sent this resolution to me and asked my support for it. So you see the resolution is not political at all, it simply means that a lot of Liberals are not less Liberals by passing this resolution; they have simply acquired a lot more sense.
We ask for the imposition of a duty on wool because we believe it is necessary to the industry. The member for Maple Creek (Mr. Swanston) told you that Saskatchewan is a splendid country for raising sheep. So it is. All the country south from Maple Creek to Willow Bunch is splendid for the raising of sheep. But it is not the only part of Canada suitable for sheep raising. I think I know Canada fairly well from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I do not know of one place in the whole Dominion where sheep raising is not natural. It is a natural industry. When I was in old Ontario long years ago, milking cows and attending to horses and doing all the work that everyone does on a farm, the raising of sheep was part of our activities. It can be made a profitable industry to-day. A report from the dean of the University of Saskatchewan declares that sheep raising is profitable. Indeed, it is the only really profitable part of the industry of agriculture that I know of to-day. Why not let us take hold of this industry and build it up for the farmers of the country?
I represent a rural constituency 125 miles by 110 miles, and in some parts of that constituency the farmers raise a great many sheep. In one part of the riding, where farmers were lured by the prospects of a railway, they are raising sheep to-day 25 and 30 miles from transportation. The farmers, of course, can always kill a sheep when they need meat, but so far they have not been able to get any advantage from their wool. They have to shear the sheep but they do nothing with the wool. Where is it? It is lying in the sheds, you will find tons of wool rotting in the backyards simply because it does not pay the farmers to take it 20 or 30 miles by truck or wagon to the railway and then pay railway

Canadian Wool Industry

charges. A reasonable amount of protection would stimulate the industry, and I therefore gladly associate myself with the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Swanston) who has moved this resolution. The hon. gentleman was brought up on a farm and he knows the industry from beginning to end; he knows the possibilities there are in wool producing. I am therefore very glad indeed to support his resolution and I hope my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) will tell me whether or not he is in favour of it.

subsubtopic: TARIFF ON RAW WOOL FOR THE PROTECTION OF HOME GROWERS
speechtext:
I am not going to prolong this discussion but there are one or two observations which I wish to make, after listening with a good deal of interest to the debate thus far. Let us see what the resolution says:.
That is the opinion of this house, it is expedient that the government of the Dominion of Canada place a duty on raw wool that would reasonably protect the Canadian wool growers.
I take it that the proposed duty on wool coming into this country is purely for the benefit of the wool growers. We all know that the woollen industry, so far as the manufacturing end is concerned, is pretty well protected; it is well taken care of. I have listened with a good deal of interest to my hon. friend from Cariboo (Mr. Fraser), who gave figures in regard to the imports of wool into Canada, and also in regard to exports. If I caught his remarks correctly, he said that we imported last year 11,358,000 pounds of raw wool and exported 5,000,000 pounds. Now, let me say to my hon. friend from Long Lake (Mr. Cowan) that I have come to certain conclusions in regard to this resolution, and when I have stated those conclusions I do not wish him to get the impression that he has converted me in any way, because he has not. I have arrived at my conclusions in a different way from hon. gentlemen across the floor. The riding I have the honour to represent in this house is largely a rural constituency engaged in mixed farming. The sheep industry is a part of its agricultural operations, and the representations that I have received from the farmers there, no matter to what political party they belong, are all the same. They are unanimous in this view, that the present government which came into power in 1930 has done absolutely nothing in their interests, nothing to promote their prosperity. Agriculture in this country is going down, and if the imposition of a duty on raw wool will help it I am inclined to support the resolution. Wool is something that we can produce. I am not very familiar with the industry as a whole but I have heard 
it said that there are certain qualities of wool that are not produced in this country- qualities suitable for certain classes of woollen goods. It is necessary, so I am told, to import these varieties. Apart from that, however, if the imposition of a duty on raw wool will help the industry 1 am inclined to favour the resolution. It may stimulate the sheep industry and the production of wool and provide the farmers of the country-and I am speaking particularly for my part of Ontario-with a market at a price that will give them a profit. There is not a single solitary article produced on the farm to-day which the farmer can sell at a profit. The price he is receiving is below the cost of production, and we should do everything we can to stimulate the industry. If agriculture does not prosper nobody in this country will prosper at all. It is all very well to talk about tariffs, and you can raise tariffs as high as you like for the manufacturers; but if the farmer has no purchasing power these tariffs are useless.
As I have said, I have arrived at my conclusions in a different way from my hon. friends across the house, and I am inclined to support the resolution. For heaven's sake let us try to do something for the farmer. I repeat, this government has done nothing to stimulate the great basic industry of the country, agriculture. We need not go further than the estimates which have been brought down. There, Mr. Speaker, you will find that the estimates for this great industry for the next year are some 83,300,000 less than they were last year. If there is any industry in connection with which the estimates should not be cut down, even in this time of stress and strain, it is agriculture. I will support this resolution and give the government of the day a chance to show that they will attempt at least to do something for the farmer. I sincerely hope that if a duty is imposed on raw wool coming into the country the manufacturers will not attempt to raise their prices. If they do it will be only a farce. However,
I take a chance on that and support the resolution.

speechtext:
I
regret that I find myself in complete disagreement with my hon. friend (Mr. Sanderson), who has just concluded his short address.
I shall have to do to him what Premier Henry did to me in the Ontario legislature the other day, I shall have to take him out in the front yard and spank him. I agree with the hon. member for Long Lake (Mr. Cowan) that this resolution involves a clear cut declaration of policy; therefore there should be no fear with regard to the outcome of the vote. I

Canadian Wool Industry
know that my hon. friends across the way always have been true to a false policy, and I anticipate that they always will be; but I do not like to see them pulling the wool over the eyes of hon. members on this side, especially in a debate on the wool question.
I should like to make passing reference to the speech delivered this afternoon by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin- (Mr. Irvine). I have followed his career for a number of years, the first time I heard him speak being back in 1921. At that time he was denouncing the evils of protection, but apparently he has been partly converted. At the present time he does not seem to know whether he is coming or going; his speech started nowhere and ended very much in the same place. After listening to his speech one of his colleagues recalled to my memory an occasion when I followed him in this house a few years ago, after he had delivered a similar address. At that time I said he was very much like the negro who was going through a deep wood during a thunderstorm. The negro kept saying: "Good Lord, good Devil, good Lord, good Devil;" he did not know into whose hands he was going to fall.
I know where I am going to stand; I am going to stand consistently by a policy of low tariff. I do not think anything will be gained by applying further tariff protection to the woollen industry. I represent a constituency which is at least half rural and I have the interests of the farmer at heart just as much as any hon. member in this house. Let us look at this thing in a general way. We all know that the sheep population of practically every country is falling off. There must be some reason: one reason is that we are changing our mode of attire. We know that wool consumption has not increased along with the population of the world. I suggest to the hon. member for Long Lake, who I understand is the Grand Kleagle of the Ku Klux Klan, that if he is sincere in this matter he should have his organization use woollen instead of cotton sheets. As a matter of fact I would forgive him if he came down here next year dressed like Mahatma Ghandi. We know that as far as the average man is concerned he subscribes to the advice of advanced science and believes that by wearing lighter apparel it will be conducive to better health. We know that as far as the female of the species is concerned in the wearing of woollen goods, the bathing suit is the last stand and there is not much left there.

speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: MANITOBA FARMERS-SUPPLY OF FEED AND SEED
subsubtopic: TARIFF ON RAW WOOL FOR THE PROTECTION OF HOME GROWERS
speechtext:
Not only is consumption falling off, but as far as our country is concerned we are not producing the right kind of material to make the finer classes of woollen goods. The National Research Council has been endeavouring to evolve a method of producing a better grade of wool, but climatic conditions are against us. No act of this parliament can change our climatic conditions. The only way we could produce a class of wool fine enough for certain manufactured products would be to grow 'our sheep under glass. If the principle of falsely bolstering up protection is right, let us follow it right through and provide a tariff high enough to permit us to grow our sheep under glass. That would assist the glass industry.
We recall the arguments which emanated from the other side of the house, and I regret to say from this side as well, during the debate on the New Zealand treaty. Our hon. friends 6aiid that all we had to do was to put up the tariff sufficiently high to increase the production of butter in order to make prosperity for the dairyman. However, other economic factors entered into the situation just as they have in connection with the wool producers. As I said, the world consumption of woollen goods has fallen off and we cannot produce in this country a salable product for export. The same applied to butter, but we did not consider that and we foolishly went ahead and put a prohibitive tariff on the importation of New Zealand butter. During the last campaign I spoke in the riding of the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Boyes). At that time I knew he was absolutely sincere in believing that the high tariff which would prohibit the import of New Zealand butter would contain remedial measures so far as the dairyman was concerned. However, we could not produce a product salable on the export market. Our cheese rated 96 per cent No. 1; our butter rated 70 per cent No. 1, and in the interests of good business naturally we sold our surplus in the form of cheese. Our cheese commanded a premium of 3 cents per pound on the Liverpool market and it was good business for us to continue to sell our surplus in that manner. But then came the false propaganda of our Conservative friends, as a result of which the importation of New Zealand butter was stopped. What was the further result? The New Zealander did not throw his product in the sea; he made it into cheese and sold that cheese in Liverpool in competition with ours. The result of the new competition was a lower price; that price was reflected in Canada and we had the anomaly of cheese at 12 cents per pound and butter at 37 cents per pound. That condition did not
Canadian Wool Industry

obtain for very long and we then turned to an increased butter production, which production was increased some 36,000,000 pounds.
This is the very thing which our friends advocate as being in the best interests of the dairy producer of Canada. At that time I pointed out that the worst thing which could happen would be for us to go on the export market with an unsalable butter product. We are now trying to sell butter which grades only 70 per cent, No. 1, and naturally we have to take an abnormally low price. We enjoyed a premium on the British market for our cheese; we had practically no competition, but the New Zealander entered the market and Doctor Ruddick, dairy commissioner, stated a short time ago that New Zealand practically had captured our market in England because we had failed to maintain a continuity of supply. We adopted the same policy which we are being asked to adopt in connection with wool; we put ourselves on an export basis with a product which was not salable. I do not think there is one intelligent member across the way who advocated that policy two years ago but who will agree that it has had a very adverse effect upon the dairy industry.
We have the same situation in connection with wool. If we stimulate the production of wool beyond the consumptive capacity of Canada, then we will be going into the export market with an unsalable product.

speechtext:
There has been such a
noise in this part of the chamber that I could not hear my hon. friend. I suggest that he make a speech after I finish.
I am dealing with the question of producing a surplus of products which is not salable on the markets of the world. I am sorry the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Gott) is not in his place, as I would have liked to point out to him another case of falsely stimulated production. A great effort was made in southern Ontario to defeat me during the last elections. I know of the propaganda that was carried on among the bean growers there. They were told that all that was needed to bring prosperity was a tariff of $1.25 on beans. 
That idea was presented to the farmer. Finally an indignation meeting was held in the riding of Elgin and on that occasion I tried to reason with about 800 men who attended, endeavouring to point out to them that if they produced an exportable surplus of their product, they could not sell on the export market because they had not the proper grades and the beans had too much moisture content. I told them that if they increased the production beyond the consumption capacity of Canada, the price of beans would be less than $1 a bushel. The tariff was applied; the production was doubled and the result was that they had a surplus of 1,500,000 bushels that would not sell on the export market. The consequence was that the price of beans, which had stood at S3, dropped down to $1 a bushel, causing a state of chaos in the bean industry. The producers, however, came back for more of the hair of the dog that bit them; they came to the Prime Minister and he gave them a dumping duty and they again increased their production. The result is that this year they are carrying 1,000,000 bushels of beans in their granaries and the price has dropped to about forty-five cents a bushel.
The same thing may be said about any other product you like to name. Although the tobacco manufacturers told the producers there was too great a production and that they could not consume it, the producers came to the government asking for an increase in the tariff. For what purpose? In order to produce more, although the market will not absorb the present production. It is a time we called a halt to this uneconomic state of affairs. Production is increasing at the rate of 20 per cent due to the policy advocated in this very resolution, while the world population is increasing at the rate of only 5 per cent. That is why we have this state of chaos at the present time. We will yet go through a process of elimination and the country with too high a cost of production will be put out of business.
The other day we had a debate on the bonus on wheat. That bonus was given obviously for the purpose of stimulating the production of wheat. We know at the present time we have a world surplus of wheat. If it is a sound policy for us to dip into the public treasury to stimulate the production of wheat, it follows it is good policy for every other country to do likewise. If as a result of the policy endorsed by this government every country adapts the same idea, and instead of a 500,000,000 bushel surplus we have a 1,000,000,000 bushel surplus, is that going to help the basic producer? It certainly will not.

Canadian Wool Industry
I believe the farmers of southern Ontario are thoroughly convinced they cannot exploit anybody else and that is the whole purpose of dangling the protection bait before the farmers, telling them: You vote for us and we will give you a tariff. They have had a fine example of the policy of the government and they are thoroughly sick of it.
As regards the men to whom the government are giving special privileges, I can refer to the gasoline industry which to-day is exploiting the basic producer. The agricultural machinery industry, as a result of tariff concessions granted recently, has increased the price of repairs on machinery. I could refer to anything else you want to name. If you want to do something for the farmers, stop this exploitation that is talcing place at the present time. I have under my hand some letters I received to-day from southern Ontario. One man tells me that as a result of the policies of this government which have brought about trade restriction, which have lost markets for him, and which have increased the cost of everything he has to buy, so far as production is concerned the only thing he can get at to-day is his poor hired help. He says that in his neighbourhood at present married men are working for $25 a month and they are trying to maintain at the proper standard of living a family of six or seven. Can you picture a condition of that kind-a married man, in some cases where the wife has to help with the milking morning and night and the man has to feed and clothe seven children and send them to school? Do the government think they are helping that man by adding to his burden an increased cost of living? We are on the wrong track completely and the sooner we reverse the processes of all governments and have some regard for the fundamental law of supply and demand, for the cost of production and for the masses to-day who are being exploited, the sooner we shall make this world a better place in which to live.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first time that I find myself in accord with the sheep raisers. I have been engaged in the live stock industry for half a century. It is well known that the sheep men and the cattle men never agree on the ranges; they have quarrelled since the beginning of time; but in this case, when I find the raw product going out of the country to be fabricated elsewhere, I have to be in accord with this resolution. I endorse the resolution because the sheep raising industry has practically petered out. The sheep brought in from Montana under the policy pursued by my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) were sold at ridiculously high prices to many settlers in my constituency; they were sold at $14 a head when they were worth only $6, and this resolution is intended to help those men to get out of the hole in which they found themselves by being loaded with sheep at such exceedingly high prices. These sheep were brought from Montana into western Canada with the idea of eradicating the weeds from the farms that the wheat growers had been working. I do not want to tackle the wheat grower again, but by mining the soil he had been growing nothing but weeds and it was for the eradication of those weeds that the idea was formed of bringing in the sheep.
I want to have it understood that I am in favour of this resolution; I wish to have our raw products manufactured at home. I do not want to see them leaving our shores to be fabricated in other countries. It would make one's blood run cold to stand on the platform in the Winnipeg, Toronto and other Canadian stockyards and see the growing yearly steers going out of the country to be made into meat products in the United States, the beef being shipped back to Canada and used in some of the principal hotels. I do not want to see that. I am in favour of any measure on this side of the house that will keep the raw products of Canada in Canada and have them fabricated in this country. Therefore I associate myself with the resolution.

speechtext: I have lived in Canada for sixty-two years; I have lived under every government from Macdonald down to the present Prime Minister, and every time there was a fair tariff, not an exploiting one, this country has prospered. My hon. friend opposite had a tariff. What about the countervailing duties they were going to impose? They had a tariff but they camouflaged it. They tried to make the people believe: Oh, we are free traders. Why, there is not a Cob-denite or John Bright amongst my hon. friends opposite, not even the hon. member for Wey-bum (Mr. Young).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friends opposite for the past two or three years have been carrying on a campaign urging people to buy made in Canada goods. It is interesting from this side of the house to watch the development of that idea. At first the cry was: Buy goods made
Canadian Wool Industry

in your own country; buy goods made in Canada. This met with a measure of success. Now it has gone one step further and the cry is:	Buy goods made in your own province.
This afternoon I listened to the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Stanley) speaking to this resolution. His chief concern seemed to be to build up a woollen industry, not in Canada, but in Alberta. What he wants really is interprovincial tariffs to shut out from Alberta the competition of woollen producers in the east. That same policy of buy-in-your-own-province has taken hold in Saskatchewan. The friends of my hon. friends opposite are in power there and they are preaching "Buy goods made only in your own province." Today they are taking advantage of the plight in which the farmer finds himself to force him, through the Saskatchewan Relief Commission, to burn only Saskatchewan coal whether his stoves are suitable for it or not. I wonder how my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Stewart) who is supporting this resolution likes that. How do my hon. friends like the policy of buy home made goods carried a step further when it is confined to their own province? The next logical step in this policy of theirs would be: Buy only goods produced in your own family. When we reach that stage it is only a step to Gandhi and the spinning wheel, and if they could bring us to that pass , they would lower the standard of living in this country to what it is in India.
In September, 1930, a special session of this house was called for the purpose of raising tariffs. That session was brought to a speedy close because the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) wanted to get to the Imperial conference in England, an imperial conference called for the purpose of promoting inter-empire trade. One of the first things we did during the short session was to raise the duty on New Zealand butter, and the very day we did it the Prime Minister of New Zealand sat on the floor of this house and watched it done. He went away from here in rather an unfriendly mood. The Imperial conference proved to be a fiasco.

My hon. friends opposite
promised to raise the price by means of a duty, which they utterly failed to do. The same thing happened with eggs. The duty on eggs coming in from the United States was three cents. My hon. friends opposite told the farmers that they were not getting a high enough price for their eggs because the duty was not high enough. They were returned to power and raised the duty to ten cents, and what was the result? Eggs two years ago in January were selling in the west for 40 cents a dozen. When I left home this year they

Canadian Wool Industry
were selling for ten cents a dozen, and that is fresh laid eggs. Did the duty raise the price? No. Did it hold the price up, did it prevent it from going down? No. Then they put a duty of thirty cents a bushel on wheat. What for? To shut out less than one million of bushels of a certain kind of wheat brought in for special purpose. When they did that the price of wheat was in the neighbourhood of 90 cents a bushel; to-day it is in the neighbourhood of 60 or 70 cents. Again I ask, did the duty hold up the price? Again it failed.
My hon. friend from Lethbridge mentioned to-day the case of mutton. A duty was put on mutton last year to hold up the price. What happened? Mutton on his own admission is lower to-day than it was then. Now since the tariff has failed to hold up the price of butter, since it failed to hold up the price of eggs, since it failed to hold up the price of wheat, since it failed to hold up the price of mutton, since it failed to hold up the price of beans since it has failed to hold up the price of practically everything on which it has been applied of the products which the farmer has to sell, what reason have we to think that a tariff of 34 cents or any other rate will hold1 up the price of wool?

speechtext:
Wherever you have an exportable surplus of a staple commodity, and that surplus is sold in the world's market, the world price fixes the price of the domestic article, but wherever you have a commodity that can be sold within a sheltered market with outside competition shut out, as is the case with manufactured goods, then the seller of those goods is in a position to take advantage of the tariff to boost the price, as he does.
We were told this afternoon, and figures were quoted by hon. gentlemen opposite, that we export approximately five million pounds of raw wool. If you put a duty of 34 cents a pound on raw wool, what effect will it have on the price? Those five million pounds of export wool will be sold on the world's market, and the world price will determine the price that we will pay for wool in Canada. So the price will not advance one cent.
My hon. friends say that they will shut out the wool that is imported and supply the demand with the wool that we now export.
But they will not do that for the reason that it is not the same kind of wool. They told us that the Canadian woollen manufacturers have assured them that the Canadian wool is suitable for the fabrics they produce. So it is. But it is not suitable for the fabrics they do not produce, and that is the reason they do not produce them. Canadian wool is suitable for certain fabrics, but with all their enthusiasm for made in Canada goods I wonder how many of my hon. friends opposite would like to come into this chamber in a suit of homespun, made of all Canadian wool. I wonder how many would like to wear a suit of underwear made altogether of Canadian wool. Is there any difference between Canadian wool and other wool? Yes. It is not due to the breed of the sheep. It is due to our climate. Our climatic conditions are such that our sheep grow a wool which is suitable for certain purposes but not suitable for other purposes, and the wool we export is the surplus wool we have over and above our own requirements for the purpose for which that wool is suited. The wool we import is wool fhalt we require for making goods that cannot 'be made with our own wool.
Reference was made to the price we pay for this foreign wool, as compared with the price we receive for our own wool. I asked the hon. member who was speaking a question, and he said that we get the foreign wool cheaper. That is not the case. I have here the 1930 price of foreign and domestic wool. The price of western Canadian range wool was 16 cents a pound. That was the average price paid that year. The price for the cheapest kind of imported wool in the grease was 33 cents a pound, more than twice as much as the price of the domestic wool. This year the average price of imported wool in the grease is 20 cents a pound, and hon. gentlemen opposite have been telling us all day that the price of our Canadian wool is from 5 to 8 cents a pound. I ask this question:	Why does the Canadian woollen
manufacturer pay twice as much for imported wool as he would have to pay for Canadian wool? Why does he do that? Is it because he is prejudiced against the Canadian wool grower? Not at all; he is a practical business man. He pays a higher price for that wool because he requires it for his purposes, and no duty which can be placed on imported wool can force him to buy Canadian wool for purposes for which it is not suited.
Let us suppose that a duty is applied; what will happen? Either it will or it will not increase the price of wool. It it does not increase the price of raw wool to the farmer
Canadian Wool Industry

what good is it? If it increases the price of raw wool to the farmer it increases the price the manufacturer has to pay for his raw wool. What will the manufacturer do? He will be back to-morrow knocking at the door of parliament asking for a higher duty on finished woollen goods. How would the government refuse him?
What are the chief competitors of wool?- cotton, rayon, silk and other fabrics. If the government did anything to advance the price of wool they might tax it right off the backs of the people and force them to wear articles composed of other fabrics. I suggest we cannot help the woollen industry by increasing the price of woollen goods. England tried that in the seventeenth century. Because her sheep growers were most influential she was resolved at all costs to build up her woollen industry. She resorted to every conceivable device, such as import and export duties. She passed laws stating that all other fabrics such as silks and cottons imported into the country must be exported so that the people would be forced to wear woollen goods. She passed laws compelling people to be buried in woollen shrouds. What was the result? She failed utterly to build up her woollen industry; she forced the people to use cotton. So far did she carry out her attempt to protect the woollen industry that a continental observer in England wrote to this effect: "It is a felony in England to export wool; yet they who furnish all the world with wool have the least manufacturing of it among themselves." What happened? The English weavers who were denied the use of imported wool had to weave their cloth out of domestic wool? The French weavers who had the world from which to select were able to choose finer wool, produce a finer fabric which drove the English woollen goods out of every market in the world. At the same time the price of woollen goods in England rose so high that the people turned to the wearing of cotton, and the woollen industry which the government was trying to build up by artificial means was utterly ruined.
What is the remedy for the woollen situation to-day? We say that people are not wearing as much wool as they used to; that is true. The fact is however that Canadian wool is not to any great extent used in the manufacture of garments. Its use is confined chiefly to the making of blankets and other coarser woollen products. I should like to take some of my hon. friends opposite into some of the houses which are not heated with steam, and where the occupants are not quite

as comfortable as are my hon. friends, and show them how many of those people would like to have woollen blankets, but cannot afford them. How many people are sleeping between cotton blankets because they cannot afford wool? To create a larger market it is necessary to put woollen goods upon the market at a lower, rather than a higher price.

Mr. Speaker,

Canadian Wool Industry
ber for Wetaskiwin gave his assent. The resolution, with which I heartily agree, is as follows:
Whereas, the fiscal policy known as protection or a protective tariff which has been on trial in Canada for over fifty years since its inauguration in 1879, has belied every promise of its promoters, both then and since, and has utterly failed to promote the general well-being of the people of Canada and has developed instead a most pernicious maldistribution of our wealth, and is on this account immediately responsible for that disparity in market values as expressed in present day prices, which exists between what the farmer sells and what he buys, which disparity is one of the principal causes of the present industrial debacle and the general economic depression;
Be it therefore resolved, that the time has come for an immediate all round reduction in our custom duties to the intent that within a period of not less than five years every feature and constituent of this barbaric economic superstition be eliminated from the fiscal policy of our country.
I repeat; I presume the hon. member for Wetaskiwin gave his consent to that resolution?

subsubtopic: TARIFF ON RAW WOOL FOR THE PROTECTION OF HOME GROWERS
speechtext:
Hearing the hon. member's speech I was reminded of the Irishman who was willing to sign the pledge, with certain exceptions-that he might indulge at a wedding, at a wake, at the market or a fair, or "when I think I need it". So it occurred to me that some people are strongly opposed to the principle of protection except when they think they need it. Hon. members opposite evidently are utterly unable to understand that those representing farmer constituencies should be opposed to this resolution. Listening to the arguments advanced in its support, I was taken back to my boyhood days. The first knowledge I had of political affairs was gained in the election of 1878. I remember we were hearing then the very same arguments for protection on wool that we are hearing to-day. Personally I am convinced the farmer is on the wrong track when he commits himself to the principle of protection. He may secure some immediate temporary advantage, but ultimately it will be to his disadvantage. Surely we have had abundant results to confirm that. If anything should warn the Canadian farmer of his danger, it is the experience of the farmer in the United States. He has been urged again and again to support the principle of high protection, and he has yielded. What is the condition of the American farmer to-day? Has he benefited because of his adherence to the principle of protection? No, his acceptance of that principle has been to his complete disadvantage.
I am satisfied that if the condition on the farm is to be what we want it to be we must seek the remedy along entirely different Lines; we must seek it along the lines of reducing the cost of production rather than increasing the price of the product that we have to sell, for in a general way that price is beyond our control. Surely we have had experience enough in the case of butter to show that a protective tariff in itself does not give the farmer the returns to which he is entitled. We have listened so frequently to the arguments from the other side of the house, that having seen those arguments so falsified one is amazed that they should be repeated to-day.
When addressing the house the other day I said I had a message that I wanted to deliver to the member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins).
I did not do so on that occasion because he was not present. I am going to deliver it to him now. I have received a letter from a friend of mine telling me that he had just sold a 10 gallon brimful can of table cream-the highest grade of cream-that tested 32 per cent butter fat, for which he received $2.85. Now, I should like to say to the member for Marquette, and to all those other members from the west who during the election campaign went around the country showing cream cheques-the member for Souris (Mr. Willis) was one; I think probably all the Conservatives in Manitoba did the same-I want to say to them that some of those 1930 cheques would look mighty good to-day.
Those who support this resolution are, I submit, proceeding along wrong lines. The only effect it can have if translated into practice is as was pointed out by the hon. members for West Elgin and Weyburn; and in spite of the inability of the member for Long Lake (Mr. Cowan) and other members opposite to understand that we who are interested in the prosperity of the farmer take the position we do, I am compelled, Mr. Speaker, to stand by the position I have always taken,-that the farmer is on the wrong track when he seeks to increase his profits by means of a protective tariff.

subsubtopic: TARIFF ON RAW WOOL FOR THE PROTECTION OF HOME GROWERS
speechtext:
I desire, Mr. Speaker, to associate myself with this resolution. I am a practical farmer; that is the way I make my living. I am fairly welt acquainted with sheep, with cattle and with hogs and with every other line of agriculture that the farmers are attempting to carry on at the present time.
Farming has changed considerably in the last ten or fifteen years. I speak with reference to the maritime provinces, particularly my own province of Prince Edward Island, one of the counties of which I represent. At one time our chief agricultural industry on the island was the growing of hay and coarse grains for export to the cities of central Canada and to the different markets of the world. The motor car has changed all that; it has driven the horse off the streets of our cities and of every other city in the world. In a word, the motor car has supplanted the horse and has changed our transportation methods. Now we have to change too. Instead of attempting to put our hay and coarse, grains on the market in their raw state, I thought the best thing for us to do was to turn them into something that man could eat or wear, but I am getting very little encouragement in my line of business, especially from hon. members on the other side of the house.
With reference to the sheep industry, let me point out to the house that the sheep is one of the most important animals on the farm. It is good for three things: first, we can produce from its carcass the finest meat that you can put on a man's table; second, its fleece can be fabricated into cloth for garments; third, as an aid to the farmer in the eradication of weeds it is second to none amongst domestic animals on the farm. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, anything that can

be done by this house to increase the number of sheep in this dominion and, incidentally, the profits of those who are engaged in the raising of sheep, would be of substantial benefit to the Canadian people.
A great deal has been said about butter, and I notice that my hon. friends on the other side of the house always curl up a little bit when butter is mentioned. I do not wonder ait that because they rather slipped up on this question at one time. I am surprised that they even want to put it on their bread, it was so bad to them about July 28, 1930. But with reference to the butter situation as I see it, it is quite true that we are selling our butter to-day below cost of production; but we are selling below cost of production everything else produced on the farm. And we are no worse in that regard than the farmers of every other country, so far as I know. We are told by men engaged in other walks of life that they too are sharing in the hard times. The manufacturer of the very farm machinery that has been talked about to-night tells you that he cannot make a profit; indeed, he is not merely standing still but is going behind. That is what I have been told by the dealers with whom I have talked. But to come back to the question of butter, as I pointed out a moment ago, if we cannot market our raw material in its present state-hay, coarse grains and so on-what are we to do with it? My idea is that we must turn it into food and clothing for mankind. A year or two ago we were importing from New Zealand 40,000,000 pounds of butter in one year. To-day we have had to turn our attention to the making of butter ourselves. Now, I do not know what the duty did or did not do; I am not interested in that. But the fact is that this year we have increased our own Canadian make of butter by 30,000,000 pounds. And remember, I am talking from the standpoint of the farmer. If the Candian consumer had continued this year to eat New Zealand butter what would I have done with mine? It is true it is cheap, but would it not have been cheaper still? What could I have done with my butter if the Canadian consumer had continued using New Zealand butter? Perhaps my friends on the other side will take credit for the fact that they themselves were instrumental in shutting out New Zealand butter. I give them all credit. But when we see the same thing in connection with wool as we saw in regard to butter, I think our hon. friends opposite should be fair enough to support the resolution before the house.

Canadian Wool Industry

maintopic: MANITOBA FARMERS-SUPPLY OF FEED AND SEED
subsubtopic: TARIFF ON RAW WOOL FOR THE PROTECTION OF HOME GROWERS
speechtext: I have no doubt that all that has been said with regard to the troubles of our wool producers is true. Their condition is the same as that of every other agriculturist throughout the country. They cannot make anything out of their wool at the present prices, nor can the producers of any other farm products make a profit under present conditions and at present prices. But I am surprised indeed that even one of our friends opposite should venture at this time to bring in any resolution proposing a further tariff on agricultural products after the example we have had of what has happened. Some of my colleagues on this side have fully discussed the question of butter and eggs, and we are not forgetful that last year, when dealing with the duty on corn, we were told that the price of barley was going to be so enormously increased that we could keep out com coming from the Argentine for feed purposes, as the farmers would turn to barley as feed instead of corn.

maintopic: MANITOBA FARMERS-SUPPLY OF FEED AND SEED

speechtext:
Will you
please sit down? You will have your chance to speak if you wish to. We know what the result has been as regards the effect of the duty on corn. The price of barley is even yet below cost of production; the imposition of a duty on corn had no effect. As my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) has said, the main trouble with the woollen industry to-day is not the need of a tariff, but the fact that rayon silk and similar fabrics are being used in place of wool products. In this resolution we are merely asked to give the patient, the farmer back on the prairie who is struggling to make ends meet, a little more of the medicine that made him sick. That is really what we are doing. In other words, it is just another move by a tariff-mad government to add a little more to the burdens of the farmers.
I am not going to deal with the question of a tariff on butter and eggs. Some of my colleagues, I must confess, have stolen most of the ammunition which I had prepared. There is, however, one question to which I will refer briefly, and that is the entirely different effect that tariffs have on the trade of the country. That has been shown quite clearly in the last year and a half since that short session of 1930 at which the tariff was raised, and my views are fully expressed in an editorial which I clipped from the Toronto Star of April 22, 1931. This is what they say with regard to the effect of a tariff:
Since the Bennett government introduced its high tariff legislation at the special session last autumn twenty-three countries have taken retaliatory tariff action against Canada. Belgium will, it is said, be the next. If, in half a year, one-third of all the countries with which this country has been carrying on her world trade have taken retaliatory tariff action against us most of the forty other countries with which we have been doing business will probably be getting back at us before the year is out.	.
There is a tendency in all countries to answer blow for blow in this tariff war.
I am opposed to any further imposition of a tariff on farm products, for this reason, that everything which the farmer produces is a drug on the market to-day, it matters not what it is, and this is due largely to tariffs, as this editorial states. We restrict the products of other countries by a high tariff and the result is that we cannot sell to tnose countries. I cannot support the resolution because to my mind it will have the same effect that tariffs have always had-it will increase the price of woollen clothing and other products made from wool.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on this resolution but I feel I must express my approval. It is rather hard for me to understand the opposition of agricultural members from Saskatchewan. I wonder if some of the hon. members of the opposition will not agree with me that one of the principal reasons in the drop of the price of our wool is the effect of the tariff put into force by the country to the south of us. That explains why the price of our wool went down. No hon. member, especially of the opposition, has referred to the agriculturists of Great Britain and what became of them because of the policy of free trade. I think all hon. members will be ready to acknowledge that it about wrecked the agriculturists of that country. The last
Canadian Wool Industry

elections demonstrated the results which the farmer of Great Britain had been obtaining through free trade.
I am rather surprised to hear hon. members declare that they never will endorse protection. The principle of tariffs was in force long before this government came into power. I would refer hon. members to Germany, France, Italy and those countries which put up tariffs amounting to as much as SI.80 per bushel against our wheat. I attended a meeting in my constituency and I was asked to explain why a tariff against wheat coming into Canada from the United States would be of any assistance in view of the fact that both countries were exporters of this product. I was very glad to have an opportunity of answering a question like that. If I remember rightly, in 1929 a tariff of 12 cents per bushel was in force against American wheat. For four or five months the Winnipeg market was leading by 21 cents per bushel, and I think the opposition will agree that a considerable amount of wheat was bootlegged into Canada to be sold on the Winnipeg market. There was an advantage in price even though both countries were exporters.
I feel sure that the hon. members of this house are in accord that something should be done to help the producers of wool. One hon. member has said that wheat has been a great boon to the farmer; I endorse that, but I do not know of any animal on the farm which gives a greater return than does the sheep.
In view of what has been said I have come to the conclusion that it is pretty hard to convince any man against his will, even though he may think as you do. It looks to me as though certain hon. members of the opposition feel that this policy is right, but it would be going against their will to give some benefit to the producers of sheep in western Canada.

maintopic: MANITOBA FARMERS-SUPPLY OF FEED AND SEED
subsubtopic: TARIFF ON RAW WOOL FOR THE PROTECTION OF HOME GROWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the very able and thorough presentations which have been made on this subject matter by the mover and seconder of the resolution, there is very little left to be said. It is not my intention to speak at any great length, as tariffs are not directly under my department.
I must admit that I admire one characteristic of hon. gentlemen opposite, that is the ability to speak with an apparent conviction based on a logic which they cannot really accept. Speaker^ after speaker, not only in this but in previous sessions, has risen in his place and inferred at least, if he has not made the definite statement, that the reduction in the price of butter, eggs and some other commodities has been due to the tariff. I would fMr. Loucks.]
like to see hon. gentlemen follow that logic one step further and apply it to the commodity with which we are dealing to-night. I believe I am safe in saying that the drop in the price of wool has been greater than that of any other agricultural commodity. The sheep industry of Canada has been practically at a standstill right from its inception. In 1871 the sheep population of Canada was in the neighbourhood of between three and four million head, and the present day population is about the same; there has been very little change or fluctuation throughout the sixty years.
The sheep ranchers and farmers of the Canadian west take second place to none. I met some of these men last summer in Lethbridge and I was very much impressed by their intelligence and the amount of care they had exercised in carrying on this industry. But in what condition do they find themselves to-day? On this side of the line the price received for wool in the grease is from 4 to 6 cents per pound, while the American farmer is receiving from 15 to 18 cents per pound for wool of a similar grade and character. Will any hon. member say that if the tariff in the United States was removed the price would remain where it is to-day? The tariff must have a bearing on the price of wool or it would not be where it is to-day.
In 1921 when the American government first put on anything like a fair tariff on wool only 49 per cent of the total wool consumption was domestic. The tariff was increased in 1930, up to which year there had been a continuous increase in the percentage of domestic wool, finally reaching 89 per cent. Figures are available only for eleven months in 1931, but they show a higher percentage of domestic wool being used in the total consumption than for any year during the last thirty years. It must be admitted that the tariff has kept up the price of wool in the United States and has also increased the percentage of domestic wool used in home consumption.
The sheep growers, who know whereof they speak, claim that they cannot continue in the industry should prices remain at their present levels. Is it worth our while to do something to keep alive this industry into which these men have put so much? Personally, I feel that it is. If they were not efficient it would be a different thing, but they are as efficient as the sheep farmers of any country in the world. I have no hesitation in stating that we should put forward every effort to keep this industry alive.

Canadian Wool Industry
The resolution asks that a tariff be placed on raw wool. That alone would not be sufficient to protect the wool industry. I feel that any tariff that will protect the wool industry must be on the whole schedule of wool from wool in the grease, wool scoured, wool tops, yarns and so forth. I therefore appreciate this opportunity to put myself on record as being in favour of the resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MANITOBA FARMERS-SUPPLY OF FEED AND SEED
subsubtopic: TARIFF ON RAW WOOL FOR THE PROTECTION OF HOME GROWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for reasons which will be obvious when my voice is heard in this chamber, my remarks must of necessity be exceedingly brief, but I feel it is incumbent upon me to say a few words with respect to the subject matter of the resolution, even in the present condition of my voice.
Let me at once compliment the mover (Mr. Swanston) and the seconder (Mr. Stewart, Lethbridge) of the resolution upon the excellence of their presentation and upon the wealth of material which they have brought to bear upon their argument and discussion. Indeed, it has occurred to me that the discussion, particularly on the part of the proponents of the resolution, has been conducted throughout on a very high plane, with exceptional credit to those who have participated. I say "proponents" of the resolution, because I could not help feeling that I was on old and familiar ground in listening to the arguments of some of my hon. friends opposite. I was at pains to follow the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) who demonstrated to a reductio ad absurdum that a duty upon wool would have the effect of lowering the price to the farmer and therefore would be disastrous to the industry. Apparently his argument found favour among those who surround him. But if you please, sir, almost in the same moment an hon. gentleman who sits but a few feet from him, the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young), proceeded to demonstrate that the placing of a duty upon wool would have the effect of increasing the price to such an extent that it would be too expensive to use and people would have to resort to cotton. I could not help thinking that hon. gentlemen opposite, as illustrated in the two speeches to which I have referred, were absolutely consistent in their characteristic inconsistencies. But, that while this inconsistency came from two different hon. gentlemen opposite, they at least were in far better position than those gentlemen of their party whom I used to -hear twenty-one years ago demonstrate upon the platform that reciprocity with the United States was going to get the farmer higher prices and the consumer cheaper commodities.
I do not propose to enter into a discussion as to the merits of the resolution, but I could not help making this brief reference to the position-I might say, to the juxtaposition- of hon. gentlemen opposite. There must be something wrong with an industry which today, with a population in Canada of more than 10,000,000, has only as many sheep as there were sixty years ago when our population was just one-third of what it is now. The argument presented by the proponents of this resolution impressed me very favourably. There is a time-honoured custom as to the method whereby announcements with ' respect to the tariff are made, and it is not incumbent upon me to make any pronouncement now as to what it is the intention of the government to do.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no intention
whtever of participating in this debate, but when I hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) and the newly appointed Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) take the stand which they have taken to-night, I feel that I should say something. I should like first to congratulate the Minister of Finance on his elevation to his present position. His appointment has been pleasing to every member of the house. We note with pleasure the manner in which he discusses any question with which he chooses to deal. He has always that fine, soft smile we like to see from any person, even if he happens to be saying things he may not approve.
But the point I should like to make is this: if the imposition of a duty on wool is something which ought to be done in order to aid the industry of agriculture, and in particular the sheep growers of this country, why have the members on the government side been silent as the grave for seventeen months until the third session of this parliament? Why have these two ministers of the crown been silent during all that time respecting the matter? Is it because, as I happened to say over twelve months ago, this is a one-man government with a following so meek and submissive one would almost think a condition of hibernation had taken possession of them? I am not going to discuss the matter at length, but I should like to say this: I have not heard all the discussion to-day, but I have heard hon.
Canadian Wool Industry

gentlemen opposite time and time again discuss this question of protection and the principle of protection. I believe the words of Thomas Carlyle are as true to-day as the day they were uttered when he said:
During these many years I have heard no argument for it excepting such as might make the angels and even the very jackasses weep.
